Hand a sample to the survey package

Source: R/survey.R
as_svydesign.Rd

Builds a survey::svydesign() object from a drawn sample, so that the survey package can do the analysis this package does not, such as regression, calibration and analysis with replicate weights.

Usage

as_svydesign(sample, ...)

Arguments

sample

A data frame returned by draw() with weights = TRUE. See "Weights and design columns".

...

Passed to survey::svydesign() by name, and an unnamed argument is refused. Anything named here overrides what the mapping above would have supplied, so nest = TRUE or a replacement fpc is yours to set.

Value

A survey.design object.

Details

The two packages compute variance from different starting points. This one uses the design's inclusion probabilities; survey reconstructs the variance from the design's shape. So the job here is to express each design in survey's own terms rather than hand over a weight column and hope.

What maps to what

DesignExpressed asStandard errors
design_simple(), design_spatial()ids = ~1 with fpc the rows the design can reachidentical
design_reservoir()ids = ~1 with fpc the rows the stream reachedidentical
design_stratified()strata from the strata columns, fpc each stratum's sizeidentical
design_temporal()strata from the sampling intervals, fpc each interval's sizeidentical
design_cluster()ids a .cluster column numbering the clusters, fpc the number of clustersidentical
design_multistage(), and design_cluster() with balanced = TRUEtwo stages, ids the .cluster numbers then the rows, fpc the number of clusters and each cluster's size; with one sampled row from a selected cluster of several, one stage, ids the .cluster numbers and no fpcidentical
design_weighted(), "poisson"survey::poisson_sampling(), which models the random size; with strata, the strata too, which change only the degrees of freedomidentical
design_certainty()the certainty rows as one unit in a stratum of their own, taken whole, beside rest as it maps alone; over a Poisson rest, survey::poisson_sampling() from the whole sample's .probas rest
design_weighted(), "systematic"pps = "brewer" with the inclusion probabilities; with strata, strata from the strata columns and Brewer's within themclose for totals, less so for means
design_multistage() with sizetwo stages, ids the .cluster numbers then the rows, pps = "brewer" with each cluster's stage-one probability and m / N_i at the second stage; each cluster taken with certainty a stratum of its own, whose rows are its units; with one sampled row from a selected cluster of several, one stage, ids the .cluster numbers and no fpcclose; identical in one stage
design_spread()as its first-order design: ids = ~1, or pps = "brewer" with size; with strata, strata from the strata columns and fpc each stratum's size, or Brewer's within themdiffer
design_systematic() with n_starts of 2 or moreids a .cluster column numbering the replicates, fpc the n_starts * interval possible startsidentical
design_systematic()ids = ~1 with fpc the rows the walk can reachdiffer
design_stratified() with withinstrata from the strata columns, fpc each stratum's rows walkeddiffer

"Identical" means to floating point under survey's default options, and is checked by this package's tests against survey::svytotal(), as are domain estimates against survey::svyby() and degrees of freedom against survey::degf(). The exceptions are real and worth knowing:

  • Systematic PPS. Neither package has its joint probabilities. This one uses Deville's approximation and survey uses Brewer's. In simulations on frames of 100 to 300 rows with gamma and lognormal sizes, the standard errors of totals usually agreed within 0.5 percent, and within 3 percent in every sample. Those of means differed more, and more as the sampling fraction grew: typically by under 2 percent at a fraction of a tenth or a fifth, 2 to 4 percent at a third and 3 to 7 percent at a half, where single samples differed by up to 12 percent. On a frame whose units below certainty had probabilities from 0.05 to 0.95, with about 17 of them in each sample, totals differed by about 1 percent typically and by up to 9 percent, and means by 7 to 9 percent typically and by up to 17 percent. The degrees of freedom agree. With strata, each stratum is handed over the same way. design_multistage() with size meets the same two approximations at the first stage, while the variance within the selected clusters is the same in both packages. Where the clusters below certainty had stage-one probabilities of 0.12 to 0.41, the standard errors of totals agreed within 0.3 percent over 200 samples. With a cluster at 0.93 among them, survey's came out 0.97 to 1.48 times this package's: Brewer's approximation centres on the plain mean of the clusters' totals over their probabilities, which that cluster pulls, where Deville's weights each by 1 - pi.

  • Spread. survey has no estimator for a spatially balanced sample, so it is told only the first-order design and computes a variance that ignores the spreading. Relative to the true variance that errs conservative, often substantially. Relative to ht_total()'s local mean approximation it goes either way. In simulations drawing 30 of 300 points spread over a square, survey's standard error was the larger in every sample when y varied smoothly over the square, three times as large at the median. When y had no spatial pattern it was the smaller in 67 to 79 percent of samples, by 4 to 6 percent at the median, and drawing 150 of the 300 it was the smaller in every sample, by 30 percent at the median, because the local mean has no finite population correction.

  • Systematic. survey, told only ids = ~1, computes the simple-random variance; ht_total() uses the successive-difference approximation, which can see a trend along the sort order. Neither is design-unbiased, and at a step of 2 rows or more no such estimator exists for one systematic sample. Within strata, survey computes the stratified simple-random variance and ht_total() adds up the strata's successive-difference approximations. With n_starts of 2 or more the replicates are clusters and the two agree. A replicated sample with a start that drew no rows, which happens only when n_starts * interval exceeds the rows walked, is refused, because survey would count one replicate fewer.

Units taken with certainty are in every sample and add nothing to the variance: the rows above a design_certainty() threshold, strata and intervals taken whole, the units design_weighted() and design_spread() with size put at probability 1, and the clusters design_multistage() and design_cluster() with balanced = TRUE take whole when they select every cluster. Each group of them goes to survey as one primary sampling unit in a stratum of its own, with an fpc of 1, so survey gives them no variance and survey::degf() leaves them out of the degrees of freedom, as ht_total() does. For the PPS designs this also keeps them out of Brewer's approximation, which left among the other units inflated survey's standard error, by a factor of 23 on a frame with four dominant units. Beside a rest of clusters, or of the replicates of several systematic starts, the certainty rows form one more primary sampling unit. In two stages, such a unit is taken whole at the second stage too.

A sample in which every row was taken with certainty, a census, goes to survey as ids = ~1 with fpc the number of rows. Both packages then report a variance of 0, and survey::degf() gives n - 1 where ht_total() gives Inf. A sample with no rows is refused, and so is a certainty sample whose rest drew none of the rows below the threshold, whose total survey would report as exact where ht_total() reports no variance.

design_certainty() over a Poisson rest goes to survey as survey::poisson_sampling() built from the whole sample's .prob, so the certainty rows enter at probability 1 and add no variance. design_bootstrap() is refused outright — it resamples the sample, so there is no finite population for svydesign() to represent.

A stratum or interval with a single sampled row makes survey stop with "Stratum has only one PSU" unless options(survey.lonely.psu) says otherwise; ht_total() declines in the same situation. Draw at least two per stratum. Under design_multistage() with size, a cluster taken with certainty is a stratum of its sampled rows, so one that gives a single row of several is such a stratum. options(survey.ultimate.cluster = TRUE) makes survey leave out the second stage of every two-stage design, so its standard errors then differ from ht_total()'s. The agreement the table states holds under the default, FALSE.

A sample weighted conditional on the clusters selected (see "Design weights" in draw()) goes over in two stages too. survey works out each cluster's second-stage sampling fraction from the rows sampled in it, which is the take given that selection, so its estimate and standard error are those of ht_total().

One sampled row from a selected cluster of several leaves the variation within clusters unmeasured. ht_total() then falls back to the delete-a-cluster jackknife, which is the ultimate-cluster variance with no finite population correction, and survey gets that design: one stage, ids the .cluster numbers and no fpc. So does a certainty design's rest of balanced clusters, which draw() weights without regard to the clusters selected, leaving no two-stage estimator. Under design_multistage() with size the jackknife runs over the clusters below certainty, and a cluster taken whole is held fixed in a stratum of its own in both packages.

Weights and design columns

survey gets the sample's .weight column as its weights. Weights adjusted after the draw, for nonresponse or by trimming, and written into .weight are therefore estimated here, while ht_total() and ht_mean() keep to the design probabilities in .prob and warn that .weight differs. .prob itself must stay as draw() set it: it supplies the probabilities of the PPS mappings above, and a sample whose .prob was changed is refused.

Strata, intervals, cluster labels and population counts come from the copy of the frame stored with the sample, not from the sample's own columns, and are passed in the columns .stratum, .cluster, .psu, .fpc, .fpc2 and .unit. Renaming or recoding a design column in the sample after the draw does not change the survey design. Those six names are reserved: a sample with a column of one of them is refused rather than overwritten. Rename the column in the sample, which leaves the design as drawn.

Replicate weights and calibration

survey::as.svrepdesign() turns the design returned here into one with replicate weights. For samples from design_simple(), design_stratified() without within, design_cluster() without balanced, design_temporal(), design_spatial() and design_spread() without size, its jackknife gives the standard errors of ht_total(variance = "jackknife"). It stops with an error on the designs handed over with Brewer's approximation or as Poisson sampling, those of design_weighted(), design_spread() and design_multistage() with size, and design_certainty() over them, because survey builds no replicates for its own probability-proportional-to-size and Poisson designs. That is a limitation of survey. For a systematic sample, alone or within strata, it builds a jackknife that ignores the order of the walk. For design_cluster() with balanced = TRUE and design_multistage() without size it keeps the finite population correction of the first stage, which ht_total(variance = "jackknife") leaves out, and warns that it dropped the corrections after the first stage. Its variance is then the jackknife's times 1 - n / N, for n of the N clusters selected.

replicate_weights() builds replicate weights from the sample itself, for survey::svrepdesign(): the jackknife of ht_total(variance = "jackknife"), for balanced clusters and the designs handed over with Brewer's approximation too, and successive differences along the walk for systematic samples. Poisson sampling, which the jackknife understates, has none, and survey estimates it from the design returned here.

frame_totals() gives the population totals that survey::calibrate() and survey::postStratify() take, from the frame stored with the sample, over the rows the design could reach. Calibration is left to survey, on the design returned here.

See also

ht_total(), ht_mean(), replicate_weights(), frame_totals()

Examples

set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(
  id = 1:400,
  site = rep(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), times = c(200, 100, 60, 40)),
  spend = round(stats::runif(400, 10, 500))
)
s <- draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 60), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)

des <- as_svydesign(s)
survey::svytotal(~spend, des)
#>        total     SE
#> spend 108333 6758.6

# The same total, and the same standard error
ht_total(s, "spend")
#> Horvitz-Thompson total  (stratified design, n = 60)
#>   estimate 108,333.3
#>   se       6,758.57  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  94,794.29 to 121,872.4  (t, 56 df)
#>   deff     1.02  (about the same as simple random sampling)

# Now the analysis this package does not do
coef(summary(survey::svyglm(spend ~ site, des)))
#>              Estimate Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept) 286.00000   21.97916 13.0123281 3.915560e-18
#> siteb       -38.86667   42.03352 -0.9246588 3.593344e-01
#> sitec        11.66667   54.65988  0.2134411 8.318019e-01
#> sited       -72.00000   57.41243 -1.2540839 2.153146e-01
